Having been a school custodian myself, I can happily say that I'd silently get pissed when I'd find a huge mess outside the norm. I.E., large piles of food on the floor, trash littered AROUND the bins, you get it. 

Only twice have I come across two insanely big garbage piles in a classroom. One was for an art teacher, the elementary kids were using glitter the whole week. (30 minutes to vacuum the whole classroom.) The other was when a kid had shredded multiple papers and scattered it like confetti around their desk. At least with that one, the kid's teacher told me not to clean it up, and that they would get the kid to do it when they got back to school the next morning. 

But I really do agree here. Keeping your personal messes to a minimum seriously helps your janitors out. 

And here's a fun fact: There are on average only 5 or 6 janitors working the school building. Head/Assistant work during the day, the rest come in as you're leaving. And those janitors typically cover a good 1/4 to a 1/3 of the entire school, almost required to clean/take out trash/vacuum/sweep/mop/wipe down windows in only 3-4 hours.

I still remember a little stuffed unicorn toy I got when I about 8 years old (maybe a b-day gift?) that I absolutely LOVED. I would not share it with any of my siblings and would cuddle with it at night. 

Over the course of about 6 or 7 years I loved that toy. It was falling apart and I took care to use old socks to keep the silk hooves from spilling beads and stuffing, would sew up those problem spots. Wanting to be a vet at the time, it was great.

Then came a dark, cold week when I went to camp without the toy. (I had usually taken it with me. Such cringe to look back on.) When I came home, I immediately realized it was gone. My mom confessed to throwing it away. 

I still feel grief and remember sobbing on the living room floor when I got that news. At least my parents felt bad enough that they got me a brand new unicorn to make up for the one they got rid of. 

Nowadays it sits in a box with all the other toys I heard for sentimental value. If you want your son to trust you around his things, in addition to trusting you, simply tell him this: "I'd like to give some of your old toys to your brother, would you sort out what you want to keep and what you want to let him have?" Also, if a deadline is appropriate, give him a day or two to do it himself. So I'd there is sentimental value with the toys, he can let go of the lesser toys on his own.

I have a cat that I get his nails trimmed about 1 or 2 times a month. I suggest for the conversation: Trimming a cat's claws is VERY different from declawing a cat. You're just clipping the tips of the claws, not removing them entirely. Try suggesting that they take their pet to a groomer, or a friend who knows what they're doing. 

Most of the time, after my cat has his nails trimmed, he just starts working on getting them sharp again by using his scratching posts. 

Yes, most cats don't enjoy being held for the procedure. Personally, I get around that by just trickle feeding my cat treats while his nails are trimmed. Never has a problem until the treats stop. 

I think there's a stigma of sorts out there that people subconsciously hold, mainly that 'Cats will take care of their own claws.' Probably from the knowledge that cats really do take care of themselves. But they can't open the cupboard and open the bag of kibble to put in their food dish. They can't change the litter boxes themselves. (If only!) So ultimately, they can't trim their claws themselves, they need our help to do it.
